### Observed differences

- In the earlier window, activity A24 took part in about 40 in 100 traces (80 of 200), with a mean of 0.4 occurrences per trace; in the later window it took part in about 53 in 100 traces (106 of 200), with a mean of 0.53 — an increase of about 13 percentage points, with no repeated occurrences of A24 within a trace in either window. [OCC001]
- This difference is larger than in about 995 of 1000 random re-splits of the pooled data, so it is unusual for a random split, though it rests on a single indicator for a single activity. [OCC001]

### Inference

Support level: Insufficient evidence
The evidence is insufficient to infer a change in the process. Only one evidence item qualified among 99 tested units, while about 0.49 items would be expected by chance in an unchanged process; a single item is the same order as that expectation, which is what a stable process typically produces, so the high empirical strength of this one item cannot rule out sampling variation. [OCC001]

- After window: 200 traces, A24 appears in 53% of traces (106 traces), mean occurrences per trace 0.53, no recurrence.
- Observed change: 0.13 (13 percentage points in participation).
- Empirical strength: 0.995 — the difference is larger than ~99.5% of random re-splits. That's unusual for random splits.
- Screening: 99 units tested, 0.49 items expected without change. We have 1 item. Is 1 item "of the same order" as 0.49? The guidance says: "A count of the same order as that expectation (for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected) is what an unchanged process typically produces: choose 'Insufficient evidence', however large or unusual a single item looks."

So with 1 item when 0.49 is expected, that's the same order — one item when fewer than one is expected. Per the instructions, this is what an unchanged process typically produces, so we must choose "Insufficient evidence", regardless of the high empirical strength (0.995).

The instruction is explicit: "A count of the same order as that expectation (for example one or two items when fewer than one is expected) is what an unchanged process typically produces: choose 'Insufficient evidence', however large or unusual a single item looks."

So: Support level: Insufficient evidence.

Empirical strength ~99.5% means the difference is larger than in ~995 of 1000 random re-splits — unusual but a single item.

Inference: Insufficient evidence. The evidence is insufficient to infer a change in the process. One qualifying item when about 0.49 would be expected by chance among 99 tested units is within what an unchanged process produces; the high empirical strength of a single item cannot rule out sampling variation.
